---
title: "10 Statistical control charts for quality analysis"
---

## 10.1 Control charts and the 3-sigma method {#sec-charts}

The pursuit of higher quality in production processes, understood as adherence to increasingly demanding standards, has characterised the world's economies since the 1950s. From the Japanese experience came a theory of total quality aimed at the control and continuous improvement of the entire business process, towards an overall optimisation of the system. An important aspect of the pursuit of higher quality is knowledge of the process and its control, so that it meets certain conditions that translate into specific statistical criteria; for example, the description of the variability shown by the process and the possible presence of abnormal fluctuations are particularly important. For this purpose, control charts are a tool that is both very useful and easy to read.

Control charts, originally proposed by Shewhart, are simply graphs showing the evolution over time of the production process, i.e. of the output or of some of its characteristics. For example, if we are monitoring the number of defective screws produced by a machine over some periods of time, we do not want a systematic increase in defects, or in any case one that would make the analyst worry about the need to recalibrate or even repair the machine; but if defects are too numerous, the control chart will signal the anomaly with fluctuations of the process beyond specific limits, usually set at $\pm 3\sigma$ from the mean of the process itself.

In this regard, Figure 10.1 shows made-up data on the breaking strength of some nails, measured daily. The process follows an irregular pattern, increasing up to the 13th observation, but still within the acceptance limits (the dashed horizontal lines).

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.1 – Graphical description of the evolution of a process"
xx <- c(10,11,10,13,12,13,14,12,14,15,14,16,15,25,24,26,23,24,27,
        14,17,16,15,16,14,13,12,14,10,12,8,9,5,6,2)   # made-up data
plot(xx, type="l", main="Evolution of a process")
abline(h=c(8,20), lty=2)
abline(v=c(13,20,32), lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.1 – Graphical description of the evolution of a process"
#| results: hide
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

xx = np.array([10, 11, 10, 13, 12, 13, 14, 12, 14, 15, 14, 16, 15, 25, 24, 26, 23, 24, 27,
               14, 17, 16, 15, 16, 14, 13, 12, 14, 10, 12, 8, 9, 5, 6, 2])   # made-up data
idx = np.arange(1, len(xx) + 1)
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.plot(idx, xx, color="black")
for h in (8, 20):
    plt.axhline(h, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
for v in (13, 20, 32):
    plt.axvline(v, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
plt.title("Evolution of a process"); plt.xlabel("Index"); plt.ylabel("xx")
plt.show()
```

### SAS

```sas
data processo;
  input xx @@;
  t = _n_;
  datalines;
10 11 10 13 12 13 14 12 14 15 14 16 15 25 24 26 23 24 27
14 17 16 15 16 14 13 12 14 10 12 8 9 5 6 2
;
run;
proc sgplot data=processo noautolegend;
  title "Evolution of a process";
  series x=t y=xx;
  refline 8 20 / axis=y lineattrs=(pattern=dash);
  refline 13 20 32 / axis=x lineattrs=(pattern=dash);
run;
```
:::

The subsequent observations jump upwards and signal an out-of-control situation, which however returns within the limits after a few days; from then on the process drifts progressively until it crosses the lower limit at the 32nd observation. So even a simple graph of some characteristic of the good or service under study can be an excellent analytical tool.

More precisely, if $\mu$ is the mean of the process, we can define two control limits following the so-called *3-sigma* method:

$$
\text{lower control limit } LCL=\mu -3\sigma \qquad \text{and} \qquad \text{upper control limit } UCL=\mu +3\sigma
\tag{10.1}
$$

Note that if the data follow a normal distribution, the interval $\mu \pm 3\sigma$ includes more than 99% of the observations, exactly 99.73%, so the probability of a type I error is 0.0027. If we wanted to reason in probabilistic terms and set a priori a type I error probability of 0.001 (i.e. 0.1%) for each limit, the multiplier of the standard deviation would be 3.09

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
qnorm(1-0.001)
```

### Python

```{python}
print(stats.norm.ppf(1 - 0.001))
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  z = quantile("NORMAL", 1-0.001);
  put z=;
run;
```
:::

Note that, to promptly signal anomalous patterns that might lead to an out-of-control situation beyond the traditional 3-sigma limit, 2-sigma warning limits can be added, i.e. a type I error of 0.025 can be set. The application of control charts is also very interesting for public services and for the analysis of the quality perceived by the users of a service, for example health care.

## 10.2 The p chart {#sec-p-chart}

A well-known control chart is the $p$ chart for attributes, used for products that can be classified as defective or non-defective with respect to some characteristic. This does not apply only to industry: in health care, for example, one may consider whether certain thresholds for the cleanliness of premises are exceeded, and so on. The chart analyses the proportion of defective items $p$, i.e. the share of items that do not conform to specific company standards. The link with the binomial distribution, which has two possible states, is immediate. So, if the sample of items inspected has size $n$ and $D$ is the number of nonconforming units, we have $P(D=x)=\binom{n}{x}p^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}$, $x=0,1,...,n$. The share of nonconforming items is $\hat{p}=D/n$, hence $\mu_{\hat{p}}=p$ and $\sigma_{\hat{p}}=(p(1-p)/n)^{1/2}$. Consequently, if the true fraction of nonconforming items is known, we write

$$
LCL=p-3(p(1-p)/n)^{1/2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=p+3(p(1-p)/n)^{1/2}
\tag{10.2}
$$

Of course, the samples inspected are usually $m>1$, not always of the same size $n$ and, above all, the true fraction $p$ is almost never known; instead, it is estimated from the sample data as $\bar{p}=\sum_{i} D_{i}/\sum_{i} n_{i}$, giving

$$
LCL=\bar{p}-3(\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})/\bar{n})^{1/2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=\bar{p}+3(\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})/\bar{n})^{1/2}
\tag{10.3}
$$

where $\bar{p}$ is the average proportion of defective items and $\bar{n}$ the average sample size.

Suppose we take 28 samples and record the number of defective screws produced by a machine in each complete production cycle of 200 pieces; the data are in the file *viti.csv* (*viti* = screws, *difetti* = defects). We compute the average number of screws produced (here obviously 200) and the average proportion of screws not conforming to the production standards

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
viti <- read.csv2("data/viti.csv")
attach(viti)
n <- sum(tot)/28
p <- sum(difetti)/sum(tot)
n; p
```

### Python

```{python}
viti = pd.read_csv("data/viti.csv", sep=";")
n = viti["tot"].sum() / 28
p = viti["difetti"].sum() / viti["tot"].sum()
print(n, p)
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/viti.csv" out=viti dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc sql noprint;
  select sum(tot)/28, sum(difetti)/sum(tot) into :n, :p from viti;
quit;
%put n=&n p=&p;
```
:::

So there is an average defect rate of about 8.4%, with limits of 2.5% and 14.3%

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
lcl <- p-3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
ucl <- p+3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
lcl; ucl
```

### Python

```{python}
lcl = p - 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
ucl = p + 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
print(lcl, ucl)
```

### SAS

```sas
data _null_;
  lcl = &p - 3*sqrt(&p*(1-&p)/&n);
  ucl = &p + 3*sqrt(&p*(1-&p)/&n);
  call symputx("lcl", lcl); call symputx("ucl", ucl);
  put lcl= ucl=;
run;
```
:::

Figure 10.2 shows the defect rate of the screw production process and indicates a share of defects under control, with no fluctuations outside the limits

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.2 – *p* chart of defective screws"
pi <- difetti/tot
plot(pi, type="o", main="p chart", ylim=c(0.0,0.16))
abline(h=lcl, lty=2)
abline(h=ucl, lty=2)
detach(viti)
```

### Python

```{python}
def carta(valori, lcl, ucl, titolo, ylim, ylabel=""):
    """Draws a control chart with constant (scalar) or variable (vector) limits."""
    t = np.arange(1, len(valori) + 1)
    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
    plt.plot(t, valori, "o-", color="black", markerfacecolor="none")
    for lim in (lcl, ucl):
        if np.ndim(lim) == 0:
            plt.axhline(lim, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
        else:
            plt.plot(t, lim, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    plt.ylim(*ylim); plt.title(titolo); plt.xlabel("Index"); plt.ylabel(ylabel)
    plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.2 – *p* chart of defective screws"
#| results: hide
pi = viti["difetti"] / viti["tot"]
carta(pi, lcl, ucl, "p chart", (0.0, 0.16), "pi")
```

### SAS

```sas
data viti;
  set viti;
  pi = difetti/tot;
run;
proc sgplot data=viti noautolegend;
  title "p chart";
  series x=nr y=pi / markers;
  refline &lcl &ucl / axis=y lineattrs=(pattern=dash);
  yaxis min=0 max=0.16;
run;
/* with SAS/QC the same chart is obtained directly: */
proc shewhart data=viti;
  pchart difetti*nr / subgroupn=tot;
run;
```
:::

Now suppose the same firm produces bolts of various sizes in a daily quantity that varies with market demand; the data are in the file *bulloni.csv* (*bullon* = bolts produced, *rotti* = defective). We build the corresponding $p$ chart (Figure 10.3)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.3 – *p* chart of defective bolts"
bul <- read.csv2("data/bulloni.csv")
attach(bul)
pi <- rotti/bullon
p <- sum(rotti)/sum(bullon)
n <- sum(bullon)/32
lcl <- p-3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
ucl <- p+3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
lcl; ucl
plot(pi, type="o", main="p chart", ylim=c(0.0,0.06))
abline(h=lcl, lty=2); abline(h=ucl, lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
bul = pd.read_csv("data/bulloni.csv", sep=";")
pi = bul["rotti"] / bul["bullon"]
p = bul["rotti"].sum() / bul["bullon"].sum()
n = bul["bullon"].sum() / 32
lcl = p - 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
ucl = p + 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
print(lcl, ucl)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.3 – *p* chart of defective bolts"
#| results: hide
carta(pi, lcl, ucl, "p chart", (0.0, 0.06), "pi")
```

### SAS

```sas
proc import datafile="data/bulloni.csv" out=bul dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc sql noprint;
  select sum(rotti)/sum(bullon), sum(bullon)/32 into :p, :n from bul;
quit;
data bul;
  set bul;
  pi  = rotti/bullon;
  lcl = &p - 3*sqrt(&p*(1-&p)/&n);
  ucl = &p + 3*sqrt(&p*(1-&p)/&n);
run;
proc sgplot data=bul noautolegend;
  title "p chart";
  series x=gg y=pi / markers;
  series x=gg y=lcl / lineattrs=(pattern=dash color=black);
  series x=gg y=ucl / lineattrs=(pattern=dash color=black);
  yaxis min=0 max=0.06;
run;
```
:::

The bolt production process appears to be under control, except for the observation of day 26; indeed

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
pi>ucl
```

### Python

```{python}
print(np.flatnonzero(pi > ucl) + 1)     # out-of-control days
```

### SAS

```sas
proc print data=bul noobs;
  where pi > ucl;
  var gg pi ucl;
run;
```
:::

One should look for the reason behind the anomalous defect rate of the 26th sample, so as to prevent the out-of-control situation from recurring and even spreading to the rest of production.

In the bolts example, the samples inspected have variable size, which would suggest looking for control limits of variable width. Three routes are possible: ignore the variable size and compute constant limits based on the average size (the option usually adopted); build the chart on standardised values (hence with centre line 0 and limits -3 and +3); compute variable limits for each sample size, as in Figure 10.4

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.4 – *p* chart of defective bolts with variable limits"
ni <- bullon
lcli <- p-3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/ni)
ucli <- p+3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/ni)
plot(pi, type="o", main="p chart with variable limits", ylim=c(0.0,0.06))
lines(ucli, lty=2)
lines(lcli, lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.4 – *p* chart of defective bolts with variable limits"
#| results: hide
ni = bul["bullon"].to_numpy()
lcli = p - 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / ni)
ucli = p + 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / ni)
carta(pi, lcli, ucli, "p chart with variable limits", (0.0, 0.06), "pi")
```

### SAS

```sas
/* PROC SHEWHART (SAS/QC) uses variable limits by default
   when subgroup sizes differ */
proc shewhart data=bul;
  pchart rotti*gg / subgroupn=bullon;
run;
```
:::

## 10.3 The np chart {#sec-np-chart}

We could build a similar chart using the number of defective bolts instead of the defect rate, obtaining the $np$ chart. Strictly speaking, this chart should be used with samples of constant size; we therefore carry out the exercise using the information on defective pins in the same file *bulloni.csv* (*totperni* = pins inspected, *difperni* = defective pins). We build and compare the $p$ chart with the $np$ chart, whose limits are now given by $np\pm 3(np(1-p))^{1/2}$ (Figure 10.5)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.5 – *np* chart and *p* chart of defective pins"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
pi <- difperni/totperni
p <- sum(difperni)/sum(totperni)
n <- sum(totperni)/32
lclnp <- n*p-3*(n*p*(1-p))^0.5
uclnp <- n*p+3*(n*p*(1-p))^0.5
lclnp; uclnp
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(difperni, type="o", main="np chart", ylim=c(5,45))
abline(h=lclnp, lty=2); abline(h=uclnp, lty=2)
lcl <- p-3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
ucl <- p+3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
lcl; ucl
plot(pi, type="o", main="p chart", ylim=c(0.01,0.08))
abline(h=lcl, lty=2); abline(h=ucl, lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
difperni = bul["difperni"].to_numpy()
pi = difperni / bul["totperni"]
p = difperni.sum() / bul["totperni"].sum()
n = bul["totperni"].sum() / 32
lclnp = n * p - 3 * (n * p * (1 - p)) ** 0.5
uclnp = n * p + 3 * (n * p * (1 - p)) ** 0.5
lcl = p - 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
ucl = p + 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
print(lclnp, uclnp); print(lcl, ucl)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.5 – *np* chart and *p* chart of defective pins"
#| results: hide
t = np.arange(1, 33)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.5))
for a, v, lo, hi, tit, yl in ((ax[0], difperni, lclnp, uclnp, "np chart", (5, 45)),
                              (ax[1], pi, lcl, ucl, "p chart", (0.01, 0.08))):
    a.plot(t, v, "o-", color="black", markerfacecolor="none")
    a.axhline(lo, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    a.axhline(hi, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    a.set_ylim(*yl); a.set_title(tit); a.set_xlabel("Index")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### SAS

```sas
/* np chart and p chart with SAS/QC (samples of 600 pins) */
proc shewhart data=bul;
  npchart difperni*gg / subgroupn=600;
  pchart  difperni*gg / subgroupn=600;
run;
```
:::

Figure 10.5 shows the two charts; the process is under control, with the usual exception of the 26th observation. Note that when the two charts are applied to samples of identical size, and of course to the same data, they lead to conclusions that differ only in the scale of the values.

## 10.4 The c and u charts {#sec-c-u-charts}

The $c$ chart is another control chart for attributes, based on the number of defects for samples of equal size. Figure 10.6 shows the example of defective pins from the file *bulloni.csv*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.6 – *c* chart of defective pins"
c <- sum(difperni)/32
lclc <- c-3*c^0.5; uclc <- c+3*c^0.5
plot(difperni, type="o", main="c chart", ylim=c(5,45))
abline(h=lclc, lty=2); abline(h=uclc, lty=2)
detach(bul)
```

### Python

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.6 – *c* chart of defective pins"
#| results: hide
cmedio = difperni.sum() / 32
lclc, uclc = cmedio - 3 * cmedio ** 0.5, cmedio + 3 * cmedio ** 0.5
carta(difperni, lclc, uclc, "c chart", (5, 45), "difperni")
```

### SAS

```sas
proc shewhart data=bul;
  cchart difperni*gg;
run;
```
:::

In this case the chart is built for samples of constant size, assuming that the number of defects $X$ follows a Poisson random variable with parameter $c$ (average number of defects), $P(X=x)=e^{-c}c^{x}/x!$, $x=0,1,2,...$, hence with limits

$$
LCL=c-3c^{1/2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=c+3c^{1/2}
\tag{10.4}
$$

But if the number of defects, and hence the average number $c$, refers to several production units, say $n$, it may be useful to build the chart around the average number of nonconformities per unit, i.e. on $u=c/n$, with limits $LCL=u-3(u/n)^{1/2}$ and $UCL=u+3(u/n)^{1/2}$, thus obtaining the $u$ chart.

With the made-up data below, in the case of variable limits, we obtain the $u$ chart shown in Figure 10.7

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.7 – *u* chart of nonconformities per unit"
dif <- c(14,12,20,11,7,10,21,16,19,23) # no. of defects
nn <- c(10,8,13,10,9.5,10,12,10.5,12,12.5) # no. of units
c <- sum(dif)/10; n <- sum(nn)/10; u <- c/n; u
lcl <- u-3*(u/nn)^0.5; ucl <- u+3*(u/nn)^0.5
ui <- dif/nn
plot(ui, type="o", main="u chart", ylim=c(0,3))
lines(lcl, lty=2); lines(ucl, lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
dif = np.array([14, 12, 20, 11, 7, 10, 21, 16, 19, 23])          # no. of defects
nn = np.array([10, 8, 13, 10, 9.5, 10, 12, 10.5, 12, 12.5])       # no. of units
u = (dif.sum() / 10) / (nn.sum() / 10)
print(u)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.7 – *u* chart of nonconformities per unit"
#| results: hide
carta(dif / nn, u - 3 * (u / nn) ** 0.5, u + 3 * (u / nn) ** 0.5, "u chart", (0, 3), "ui")
```

### SAS

```sas
data carta_u;
  input campione dif nn @@;
  datalines;
1 14 10   2 12 8   3 20 13   4 11 10   5 7 9.5
6 10 10   7 21 12  8 16 10.5 9 19 12  10 23 12.5
;
run;
proc shewhart data=carta_u;
  uchart dif*campione / subgroupn=nn;
run;
```
:::

## 10.5 Control charts for variables: the X-bar and R charts {#sec-xbar-r}

Control charts for attributes are typically applied to categorical data on the presence or absence of a defect. Conversely, control charts for variables deal with quantitative data on a characteristic $X$ of the product, such as weight, volume, etc. In this case it is advisable to keep the process under control both for the mean and for the variability; indeed, control charts for variables are applied in pairs.

If the characteristic is such that $X\sim N(\mu ,\sigma^{2})$, the sample mean is $\bar{X}\sim N(\mu ,\sigma_{\bar{X}}^{2})$, where $\sigma_{\bar{X}}=\sigma /n^{1/2}$. The 3-sigma control chart for the mean then has limits

$$
LCL=\mu -3\sigma_{\bar{X}} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=\mu +3\sigma_{\bar{X}}
\tag{10.5}
$$

and, in probability terms, $\mu -Z_{\alpha /2}\sigma_{\bar{X}}$ and $\mu +Z_{\alpha /2}\sigma_{\bar{X}}$.

Generally $\mu$ is unknown and must be estimated by the mean of the sample means $\bar{\bar{X}}$; similarly, the sample standard deviation is used for $\sigma$.

To analyse variability, as an alternative to the standard deviation, one can use the range $R$, i.e. the mean $\bar{R}$ of the sample ranges. The following limits are thus defined for the $\bar{X}$ chart (centre line $\bar{\bar{X}}$)

$$
LCL=\bar{\bar{X}}-A_{2}\bar{R} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=\bar{\bar{X}}+A_{2}\bar{R}
\tag{10.6}
$$

and those for the $R$ chart (centre line $\bar{R}$)

$$
LCL=D_{3}\bar{R} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=D_{4}\bar{R}
\tag{10.7}
$$

Note the use of the specific constants $A_{2}$, $D_{3}$ and $D_{4}$, given in dedicated tables.

If the characteristic under examination follows a normal distribution, there is a specific relationship between the range and the standard deviation. If $d_{2}$ is the mean and $d_{3}$ the standard deviation of the random variable $R/\sigma$, an estimate of $\sigma$ is $\hat{\sigma}=\bar{R}/d_{2}$. Since the limits of the chart for the mean can be defined as $\bar{\bar{X}}\pm 3\hat{\sigma}/n^{1/2}$, and hence as $\bar{\bar{X}}\pm 3\bar{R}/(d_{2}n^{1/2})$, we immediately obtain $A_{2}=3/(d_{2}n^{1/2})$.

Similarly, we can write $\sigma_{R/\sigma}=\sigma_{R}/\sigma$, $\hat{\sigma}_{R}=\hat{\sigma}d_{3}$, $\hat{\sigma}_{R}=\bar{R}d_{3}/d_{2}$, $\bar{R}+3\hat{\sigma}_{R}=(1+3d_{3}/d_{2})\bar{R}$, so that $D_{4}=1+3d_{3}/d_{2}$; likewise, $D_{3}=1-3d_{3}/d_{2}$ (set to 0 when negative).

It should be stressed that the chart for the mean measures the variability between samples, while the range chart measures the variability within samples. As the formulas also show, this implies that $\sigma$ must be estimated using only the information on within-sample variability, so the usual estimator of the standard deviation computed on all the data must not be used.

We load the data in the file *molle.csv* on the stretch limit, in cm, of some sofa springs, measured 3 times in each of 10 samples. We build the chart for the mean ($\bar{X}$ or *X-bar*) based on the range (Figure 10.8)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.8 – *X-bar* chart based on the range"
molle <- read.csv2("data/molle.csv")
media <- 0; rang <- 0
for (i in 2:11) media[i-1]=mean(molle[,i])
for (i in 2:11) rang[i-1]=diff(range(molle[,i]))
centrale <- mean(media); rmedio <- mean(rang)
centrale; rmedio
A2 <- 1.023 # tabulated value for n=3
lcl <- centrale-A2*rmedio
ucl <- centrale+A2*rmedio
lcl; ucl
plot(media, type="o", main="X-bar chart via range", ylim=c(8.1,9.5))
abline(h=lcl, lty=2); abline(h=ucl, lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
molle = pd.read_csv("data/molle.csv", sep=";", decimal=",", index_col=0)
media = molle.mean().to_numpy()                       # means of the 10 samples
rang = (molle.max() - molle.min()).to_numpy()         # ranges of the 10 samples
centrale, rmedio = media.mean(), rang.mean()
A2 = 1.023                                            # tabulated value for n=3
lcl, ucl = centrale - A2 * rmedio, centrale + A2 * rmedio
print(centrale, rmedio); print(lcl, ucl)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.8 – *X-bar* chart based on the range"
#| results: hide
carta(media, lcl, ucl, "X-bar chart via range", (8.1, 9.5), "media")
```

### SAS

```sas
/* long format: one row per measurement */
data molle;
  infile "data/molle.csv" dlm=";" firstobs=2;
  input misura $ (c1-c10) (:commax8.);
  array c{10} c1-c10;
  do campione = 1 to 10;
    valore = c{campione};
    output;
  end;
  keep campione valore;
run;
proc sort data=molle; by campione; run;
/* X-bar and R charts with the tabulated constants A2, D3 and D4 */
proc shewhart data=molle;
  xrchart valore*campione;
run;
```
:::

Note that the fifth point is out of control (mean and range of the fifth sample equal to 9.4 and 0.6 respectively)

The limits of the $\bar{X}$ chart depend on the average range, so it would be preferable to check first that the $R$ chart does not signal any out-of-control points; here, however, we have preferred to follow the order of presentation.

Building the range chart is straightforward (Figure 10.9)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

uclr <- D4*rmedio

## 10.6 The X-bar and S charts {#sec-xbar-s}

The $R$ chart is preferable for small samples, but for sizes above 5 the estimate of $\sigma$ based on the range becomes progressively less precise. Generally, with $n>10$ or with variable sample sizes, a specific $S$ or $S^{2}$ chart is preferred to the $R$ chart; of course the construction of the corresponding $\bar{X}$ chart is also affected.

Let us assume, as usual, that the characteristic $X$ of the product follows a normal distribution. If $\sigma$ is known, the $S$ chart has centre line $c_{4}\sigma$, with lower and upper 3-sigma limits equal to

$$
LCL=B_{5}\sigma \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=B_{6}\sigma
\tag{10.8}
$$

where the constants $c_{4}$, $B_{5}$ and $B_{6}$ take specific values tabulated by sample size, such that $B_{5}=c_{4}-3(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}$ and $B_{6}=c_{4}+3(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}$.

If the standard deviation is unknown, it must be estimated using the relationship $\hat{\sigma}=\bar{S}/c_{4}$, where $\bar{S}$ is the mean of the sample standard deviations. The $S$ chart then has centre line $\bar{S}$, with limits

$$
LCL=B_{3}\bar{S} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=B_{4}\bar{S}
\tag{10.9}
$$

where $B_{3}=1-(3/c_{4})(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}$ and $B_{4}=1+(3/c_{4})(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}$.

The limits of the $\bar{X}$ chart (whose centre line is still $\bar{\bar{X}}$) must then also be redefined

$$
LCL=\bar{\bar{X}}-A_{3}\bar{S} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=\bar{\bar{X}}+A_{3}\bar{S}
\tag{10.10}
$$

where $A_{3}=3/(c_{4}n^{1/2})$.

We load the data on the diameter of car piston rings in the file *pistoni.csv* (5 measurements for each of 25 samples). We build the two charts $\bar{X}$ and $S$ (Figure 10.10)

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
### R

```{r}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.10 – *X-bar* and *S* charts"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5
piston <- read.csv2("data/pistoni.csv")
med <- 0; dev <- 0
for (i in 2:26) med[i-1]=mean(piston[,i])
for (i in 2:26) dev[i-1]=sd(piston[,i])
media <- mean(med); mdev <- mean(dev)
media; mdev
A3 <- 1.427 # tabulated values for n=5
lclx <- media-A3*mdev; uclx <- media+A3*mdev
lclx; uclx
B3 <- 0
B4 <- 2.089
lcls <- B3*mdev; ucls <- B4*mdev
lcls; ucls
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(med, type="o", main="X-bar chart via S", ylim=c(73.98,74.02))
abline(h=lclx, lty=2); abline(h=uclx, lty=2)
plot(dev, type="o", main="S chart", ylim=c(0,0.02))
abline(h=lcls, lty=2); abline(h=ucls, lty=2)
```

### Python

```{python}
piston = pd.read_csv("data/pistoni.csv", sep=";", decimal=",", index_col=0)
med = piston.mean().to_numpy()
dev = piston.std().to_numpy()            # sample standard deviation (n-1)
media, mdev = med.mean(), dev.mean()
A3 = 1.427                               # tabulated values for n=5
B3, B4 = 0, 2.089
lclx, uclx = media - A3 * mdev, media + A3 * mdev
lcls, ucls = B3 * mdev, B4 * mdev
print(media, mdev); print(lclx, uclx); print(lcls, ucls)
```

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 10.10 – *X-bar* and *S* charts"
#| results: hide
t = np.arange(1, 26)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.5))
for a, v, lo, hi, tit, yl in ((ax[0], med, lclx, uclx, "X-bar chart via S", (73.98, 74.02)),
                              (ax[1], dev, lcls, ucls, "S chart", (0, 0.02))):
    a.plot(t, v, "o-", color="black", markerfacecolor="none")
    a.axhline(lo, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    a.axhline(hi, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    a.set_ylim(*yl); a.set_title(tit); a.set_xlabel("Index")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

### SAS

```sas
data pistoni;
  infile "data/pistoni.csv" dlm=";" firstobs=2;
  input misura (c1-c25) (:commax10.);
  array c{25} c1-c25;
  do campione = 1 to 25;
    diametro = c{campione};
    output;
  end;
  keep campione diametro;
run;
proc sort data=pistoni; by campione; run;
/* X-bar and S charts with the tabulated constants A3, B3 and B4 */
proc shewhart data=pistoni;
  xschart diametro*campione;
run;
```
:::

The process appears to be under control.

Building the $\bar{X}$ and $S$ charts is straightforward even with variable sample sizes. The centre lines are obtained using suitable weighted means instead of simple means, while the control limits, which are also variable, are computed each time with the constants for the corresponding sample size. Finally, note that some prefer the $S^{2}$ chart, based on the sample variance, to the $S$ chart.

In addition to the classical Shewhart charts presented here, the literature has proposed many other techniques, generally more detailed and more sensitive to small shifts in the process, such as CUSUM (cumulative sum) and EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) charts; we will not dwell on them further.
